lessons.0.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 1 - 18 min
lessons.0.slides.0.description: Understanding Burgundy's position in the global fine wine market
lessons.0.slides.1.title: Burgundy: King of the Fine Wine Market
lessons.0.slides.1.content: Burgundy accounts for less than 1% of global wine production, yet its share of the fine wine market is 30–40%. Over the past 20 years, Burgundy wine prices have averaged 10–15% annual growth — far outperforming stocks, real estate, and other traditional investments. Wines from DRC, Leroy, and similar top estates have become important components of alternative asset portfolios.

lessons.0.slides.3.points.4: Secondary market: auction transactions represent ~30% of total trade

lessons.0.slides.6.title: The Rise of the Asian Market
lessons.0.slides.6.content: After 2010, Asia (especially mainland China and Hong Kong) became one of Burgundy's most important markets. When Hong Kong removed wine import duties in 2011, it became a global wine auction centre. Asian collectors' pursuit of DRC and Leroy drove prices skyward. After 2020, some capital shifted back to the West, but Asia remains a critical market.
lessons.0.slides.7.title: 🌍 Global Market Share Evolution
lessons.0.slides.8.title: 🌍 Global Market Share: Year 2000
lessons.0.slides.8.content: In 2000 the Burgundy market was dominated by Europe and the US; Asia held only 5%. London and New York were the major auction centres, and annual market transactions were ~$800 million.
lessons.0.slides.9.title: 🌍 Global Market Share: Year 2024
lessons.0.slides.9.content: 24 years later the market is multipolar: Asia has risen to 28%, the US fallen to 38%, Europe to 30%. Annual market transactions reached $5 billion — 525% growth.

lessons.0.slides.10.points.3: Liquidity: easy to resell, in demand at auction houses
lessons.0.slides.10.points.4: Provenance: clear origin, perfect storage history

lessons.1.title: Auction Market Price Analysis
lessons.1.slides.0.title: Auction Market Price Analysis
lessons.1.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 2 - 16 min
lessons.1.slides.0.description: Mastering auction price trends and valuation methods
lessons.1.slides.1.title: The Significance of Auction Records
lessons.1.slides.1.content: Auction prices are the market's most transparent indicator. In 2018, a single bottle of 1945 Romanée-Conti sold at Sotheby's for $558,000 — a world record for a single bottle of wine. These records are extreme, but reflect the scarcity and collectible value of top Burgundy. Understanding auction price trends is fundamental to investment decisions.
lessons.1.slides.2.title: 🔨 Historic Auction Record Milestones
lessons.1.slides.3.title: 🔨 Major Auction Houses and Their Focus
lessons.1.slides.3.points.0: Sotheby's: the oldest; expert in top-tier wines
lessons.1.slides.3.points.1: Christie's: high-end market; specialist sessions for named estates
lessons.1.slides.3.points.2: Acker Merrall & Condit: largest in the US; highest by volume
lessons.1.slides.3.points.4: Hart Davis Hart: Chicago-based; Midwest leader
lessons.1.slides.3.points.5: Bonhams Hong Kong: leader in the Asian market
lessons.1.slides.4.title: Auction Price vs Retail Price
lessons.1.slides.5.title: Price Index Analysis
lessons.1.slides.5.content: The Burgundy 150 Index compiled by Liv-ex (London International Vintners Exchange) tracks price movements of 150 top Burgundy wines. From 2000–2024 the index rose ~400%, far exceeding equities. In 2022–2023, the global economic slowdown caused the first correction of ~10–15%; recovery began in 2024.

lessons.1.slides.7.title: 📊 Price Influencing Factors
lessons.1.slides.7.points.0: Vintage quality: great vintages (2005, 2015, 2019) command 50–100% premium
lessons.1.slides.7.points.1: Producer reputation: DRC vs an average producer can differ 10–20 times
lessons.1.slides.7.points.2: Bottle condition: perfect condition vs low fill can differ 30–50%
lessons.1.slides.7.points.3: Provenance: famous cellar origin can add 20–30% premium
lessons.1.slides.7.points.4: Market sentiment: bull vs bear affects short-term volatility
lessons.1.slides.7.points.5: Exchange rates: strength of the dollar affects international markets

lessons.2.title: Portfolio Strategy
lessons.2.slides.0.title: Portfolio Strategy
lessons.2.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 3 - 15 min
lessons.2.slides.0.description: Building a balanced and appreciating wine investment portfolio
lessons.2.slides.1.title: Diversification Is the Key
lessons.2.slides.1.content: Don't invest all your capital in a single estate or vintage. An ideal portfolio includes: core holdings (70%) — blue-chip wines offering steady appreciation; growth positions (20%) — rising stars with potential; speculative positions (10%) — high-risk, high-reward. Spread across red and white, different villages, and different vintages to reduce risk.
lessons.2.slides.2.title: 🎯 Suggested Portfolio Allocation
lessons.2.slides.2.points.0: Core blue-chip (70%): DRC, Leroy, Rousseau in key vintages
lessons.2.slides.2.points.1: Growth potential (20%): undervalued Morey, fine-vintage Premier Crus
lessons.2.slides.3.title: Conservative vs Aggressive Portfolio
lessons.2.slides.4.title: Example Starter Portfolio
lessons.2.slides.4.content: Starter portfolio with a $100,000 budget: 60% DRC Échézeaux or Leroy Premier Cru ($50–60k); 20% Rousseau or Dujac Grand Cru ($20k); 15% Coche-Dury or Ramonet whites ($15k); 5% promising emerging producers ($5k). Target 10-year total return: 100–150%.
lessons.2.slides.5.title: 💼 Real $100k Portfolio Performance (2015–2024)
lessons.2.slides.6.title: ⚠️ Investment Principles
lessons.2.slides.6.points.0: Only buy what you know: research deeply before investing
lessons.2.slides.6.points.1: Hold long-term: at least 5–10 years to see returns
lessons.2.slides.6.points.2: Perfect storage: invest in professional cellaring at ~2–3% per year
lessons.2.slides.6.points.3: Provenance first: only buy wines with clear, documented origin
lessons.2.slides.6.points.4: Buy in tranches: don't commit all capital at once
lessons.2.slides.6.points.5: Review annually: assess portfolio performance and rebalance each year

lessons.3.title: En Primeur Market and Allocation Systems
lessons.3.slides.0.title: En Primeur Market and Allocation Systems
lessons.3.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 4 - 16 min
lessons.3.slides.0.description: Understanding Burgundy's unique en primeur and allocation mechanisms
lessons.3.slides.1.title: Burgundy En Primeur
lessons.3.slides.1.content: Burgundy en primeur wines go on sale 18–24 months after harvest (reds), or earlier (whites). The advantage of buying en primeur is that prices are typically 10–30% below post-bottling prices and allocation is secured. Drawbacks: must pay in advance; must wait 2–3 years to receive the wine; cannot taste before buying. Best suited to buying top estates in great vintages.
lessons.3.slides.2.title: 🍷 How the Allocation System Works
lessons.3.slides.2.points.0: Top estates: limited annual production, allocation-based distribution
lessons.3.slides.2.points.1: Loyal clients: long-term buyers receive priority; building a relationship takes 5–10 years
lessons.3.slides.2.points.2: Distribution chain: estate → négociant → retailer → consumer
lessons.3.slides.2.points.3: Bundle system: top wines must be purchased alongside other wines
lessons.3.slides.2.points.4: DRC allocation: must purchase the full 'Assortment' (8 wines as a set)
lessons.3.slides.2.points.5: Waiting time: new clients take 3–5 years to enter an allocation system
lessons.3.slides.3.title: En Primeur vs Spot Market
lessons.3.slides.4.title: How to Build an Allocation Relationship
lessons.3.slides.4.content: Building an allocation relationship with top estates requires: 1) find a reliable négociant or importer; 2) buy the estate's entry-level wines consistently (village, Premier Cru); 3) demonstrate professional storage capacity; 4) build a long-term relationship (5–10 years); 5) attend estate events and cellar visits; 6) prove financial credibility. DRC and Leroy allocations are the hardest to secure.
lessons.3.slides.5.title: 🔑 Path to a DRC Allocation (Typical Case)
lessons.3.slides.6.title: 💡 En Primeur Buying Strategy
lessons.3.slides.6.points.0: Vintage selection: only buy en primeur in great vintages (95+ points)
lessons.3.slides.6.points.1: Top estates first: the advantage of en primeur is greatest at the top
lessons.3.slides.6.points.2: Price comparison: en primeur price should not exceed 80% of estimated market price
lessons.3.slides.6.points.3: Merchant credibility: choose established, reputable négociants
lessons.3.slides.6.points.4: Payment terms: understand cancellation policy and payment schedule
lessons.3.slides.6.points.5: Avoid speculation: en primeur is a long-term investment, not a short-term trade

lessons.4.title: Risk Management and Exit Strategy
lessons.4.slides.0.title: Risk Management and Exit Strategy
lessons.4.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 5 - 15 min
lessons.4.slides.0.description: Identifying investment risks and formulating an exit plan
lessons.4.slides.1.title: The Main Risks of Wine Investment
lessons.4.slides.1.content: Wine investment is not without risk: 1) Storage risk — incorrect temperature or humidity damages wine value; 2) Authenticity risk — forgeries are rife, especially for DRC; 3) Liquidity risk — non-top wines are hard to convert to cash; 4) Market risk — economic downturns affect luxury consumption; 5) Tax risk — laws vary by jurisdiction; 6) Physical risk — breakage, loss, theft.
lessons.4.slides.2.title: ⚠️ Major Risk Events: Historical Cases
lessons.4.slides.3.title: ⚠️ Main Risk Categories
lessons.4.slides.3.points.0: Storage risk: improper storage can reduce wine value to zero
lessons.4.slides.3.points.1: Forgery risk: ~10–20% of fine wines in the market have authenticity concerns
lessons.4.slides.3.points.2: Liquidity risk: second-tier wines may take months to sell
lessons.4.slides.3.points.3: Price volatility: values can drop 20–30% in a recession
lessons.4.slides.3.points.4: Opportunity cost: capital locked up for 10 years misses other investment opportunities
lessons.4.slides.3.points.5: Hidden costs: storage + insurance + auction commission can total 20–30%
lessons.4.slides.4.title: Self-Cellaring vs Professional Storage
lessons.4.slides.5.title: Exit Strategy
lessons.4.slides.5.content: Successful investment requires a clear exit plan: 1) Set a target — expected return rate (e.g. 200% over 10 years); 2) Staged exit — sell 50–80% once the target price is reached; 3) Keep the classics — retain some top wines for drinking or inheritance; 4) Choose a channel — auction house (large lots), merchant (retail), private sale (large amounts); 5) Tax planning — understand capital gains tax; 6) Timing — exit at market peaks.
lessons.4.slides.6.title: 🎯 Exit Timing Indicators
lessons.4.slides.6.points.0: Target reached: preset return rate achieved (e.g. doubled)
lessons.4.slides.6.points.1: Market overheating: irrational price surge, signs of a bubble
lessons.4.slides.6.points.2: Capital needed: personal financial situation changes
lessons.4.slides.6.points.3: Drinking window: wine approaching its peak drinking period
lessons.4.slides.6.points.5: Market turning: early signs of economic recession
lessons.4.slides.7.title: 💡 Practical Risk Management
lessons.4.slides.7.points.0: Insurance: insure your wine collection (~0.5–1% of value per year)
lessons.4.slides.7.points.1: Distributed storage: never store all wines in one location
lessons.4.slides.7.points.2: Regular checks: inspect bottle condition and stock annually
lessons.4.slides.7.points.3: Documentation: keep all purchase receipts and provenance documents
lessons.4.slides.7.points.4: Authentication: have high-value wines authenticated by experts before purchase
lessons.4.slides.7.points.5: Cut losses promptly: sell problematic wines decisively when issues arise
